title: At home here
hookLine: Odysseus wept for home on Calypso's island; Heracles was at home anywhere
carry: there is work for you to do

lines: A MAN ON A ROCK, CRYING.
cards: A man sits on a rock at the edge of the sea, crying. He's on a beautiful island. A goddess loves him and has offered him a life without death.
He doesn't care. Day after day he goes down to the shore and weeps for a rocky little kingdom he hasn't seen in years. That's Odysseus, in book five of Homer's Odyssey, on Calypso's island.
Epictetus picked it up and asked an awkward question about it.

teach.b: In that same long chapter of book three, Epictetus asks whether we should take Homer at his word in everything. If Odysseus really sat and wept like that, he says, then he was unhappy, not living well.

Homer may have told it that way, but a person who can only be happy in one spot on the map has handed their happiness to geography. Epictetus isn't mocking homesickness. He's asking where we've put our peace.
Then he turns to Heracles. In the old stories Heracles traveled the whole known world on his labors, clearing out cruelty and lawlessness wherever he went.

Epictetus says he made friends everywhere, had children in more than one land, and left them without groaning, not because he didn't love them, but because he believed every human being was his kin, and Zeus the father of all.

It's the citizen of the world we met on the day of names, onoma. Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he was from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world, a kosmopolitēs. This isn't a rule against missing home.

teach.h: LOVE HOME; DON'T NEED ONLY IT.
teach.b: Epictetus doesn't say don't love your city, your street, your mother's kitchen. He says don't make them the only place you can stand up straight.
Wherever there are people, sky and a chance to act well, there is work for you to do. A hospital waiting room, a new apartment, a strange city at night.
You can be at home there too.

how: Stoic writers, Epictetus among them, speak of being citizens of the world, and some practitioners make a habit of settling into wherever they are, treating any place as a place where they can act well.

o: a citizen of the world, at home anywhere
someone who has no homeland or loyalties
someone who travels constantly for pleasure

games.q: at home here — tap the pairs.
p: weeps on the rock for home
offers him a life without death
kin to people in every land

s: Epictetus says it's wrong to love your home
he says don't make one place the only place you can be well.
the weeping scene is in book five of the Odyssey
Odysseus sits on the shore of Calypso's island and weeps for Ithaca.
Diogenes is said to have called himself a citizen of the world
Diogenes Laertius tells it: asked where he was from, he said the world.

games.q: you're Odysseus. a goddess offers you an endless, easy life on her island, far from home. what do you do?
o: sit on the shore every day and weep.
build a raft and sail home.
games.why: in book five he weeps on the shore for years, until the gods send word to let him go. Epictetus asks whether that weeping was living well.

practice: Wherever you are, let your eyes move slowly around: the light, one thing someone made with their hands, a chair, a window, a cup, and the seat or floor holding you up.
Breathe the air of exactly here, and quietly tell yourself: this, too, is a place where a person can live well. You don't have to love it; just stand in it, at home for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Kosmopolitēs, a citizen of the world: Heracles at ease in every land, kin to every person, set against Odysseus weeping on his rock. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a citizen (polites) of the cosmos; Diogenes the Cynic is said to have called himself one.

carryVoice: Your line: there is work for you to do. Love home, and still stand up straight anywhere. See you tomorrow.
